items.title: Start here
items.content:
When to get help:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call 911 for a life-threatening condition.

Full reference:
1. Check for hazards before approaching. Use protective equipment if available.
2. Check responsiveness and normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds; look for severe bleeding.
3. Call 911 or ask someone to call and bring an AED. Follow the dispatcher.
4. If unresponsive and not breathing normally (including only gasping), start CPR and use an AED as soon as possible. Give other care within your training.

Important:
If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Check for hazards before approaching. Use protective equipment if available.

Action 2 / Check responsiveness and normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds; look for severe bleeding.

Action 3 / Call 911 or ask someone to call and bring an AED. Follow the dispatcher.

Action 4 / If unresponsive and not breathing normally (including only gasping), start CPR and use an AED as soon as possible. Give other care within your training.

items.title: Not breathing — teen or adult
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 and get an AED. Start CPR immediately.

Full reference:
1. Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface.
2. Put the heel of one hand in the center of the chest and the other hand on top.
3. Press hard and fast at 100–120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep, avoiding more than 2.4 inches. Allow full chest recoil.
4. If trained, give 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. If unable or unwilling to give breaths, continue chest compressions.
5. Turn on the AED as soon as available and follow its spoken instructions. Continue until professionals take over, normal breathing returns or you cannot continue safely.

Important:
For children or babies open the corresponding child or infant CPR guide. Rescue breaths are especially important for drowning-related and pediatric arrests.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface. / Put the heel of one hand in the center of the chest and the other hand on top. / Press hard and fast at 100–120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep, avoiding more than 2.4 inches. Allow full chest recoil. / If trained, give 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. If unable or unwilling to give breaths, continue chest compressions. / Turn on the AED as soon as available and follow its spoken instructions. Continue until professionals take over, normal breathing returns or you cannot continue safely.

items.title: Not breathing — child
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 using speakerphone if possible. Start CPR; ask someone to bring an AED.

Full reference:
1. Lay the child face up on a hard, level surface.
2. Place one or both hands on the lower half of the breastbone, depending on the child’s size.
3. Give 30 compressions at 100–120 per minute, about 2 inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Let the chest fully rise between presses.
4. If trained, open the airway with a gentle head tilt and chin lift, pinch the nose and give 2 breaths, each over about one second, enough for visible chest rise. Repeat 30:2. If unable to give breaths, keep compressing.
5. Use an AED when available; follow its prompts. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or you cannot safely continue.

Important:
If alone without a phone, dispatcher activation timing depends on whether collapse was witnessed; if unwitnessed, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call and obtain an AED. Use infant CPR for a baby under 1.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / Lay the child face up on a hard, level surface. / Place one or both hands on the lower half of the breastbone, depending on the child’s size. / Give 30 compressions at 100–120 per minute, about 2 inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Let the chest fully rise between presses. / If trained, open the airway with a gentle head tilt and chin lift, pinch the nose and give 2 breaths, each over about one second, enough for visible chest rise. Repeat 30:2. If unable to give breaths, keep compressing. / Use an AED when available; follow its prompts. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or you cannot safely continue.

items.title: Severe bleeding
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 and apply firm pressure immediately.

Full reference:
1. Wear gloves or use a barrier if possible. Locate the source of bleeding.
2. Press firmly and continuously with gauze or clean cloth. If an object is stuck in the wound, press around it, not on it.
3. For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, apply a manufactured tourniquet if available and trained; follow dispatcher or device instructions.
4. Keep the person warm and monitor breathing and responsiveness until help arrives.

Important:
Do not remove an embedded object; press around it. Do not loosen an applied tourniquet.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / Wear gloves or use a barrier if possible. Locate the source of bleeding. / Press firmly and continuously with gauze or clean cloth. If an object is stuck in the wound, press around it, not on it. / For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, apply a manufactured tourniquet if available and trained; follow dispatcher or device instructions. / Keep the person warm and monitor breathing and responsiveness until help arrives.

items.title: Choking — adult or child
items.content:
When to get help:
For severe choking, call 911 or have someone call.

Full reference:
1. If coughing forcefully, encourage coughing and watch closely.
2. For severe choking in a conscious person age 1 or older, lean them forward and give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.
3. If still blocked, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts with your fist just above the navel and below the breastbone, pulling inward and upward. Use chest thrusts if pregnant or unable to encircle the abdomen.
4. Repeat until the blockage clears or they become unresponsive. If unresponsive, lower safely, begin CPR and follow the dispatcher.

Important:
Never sweep the mouth blindly. Remove an object only if visible during CPR. Never use abdominal thrusts on babies.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / If coughing forcefully, encourage coughing and watch closely. / For severe choking in a conscious person age 1 or older, lean them forward and give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades. / If still blocked, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts with your fist just above the navel and below the breastbone, pulling inward and upward. Use chest thrusts if pregnant or unable to encircle the abdomen. / Repeat until the blockage clears or they become unresponsive. If unresponsive, lower safely, begin CPR and follow the dispatcher.

items.title: Choking — baby under 1
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 or have someone call. Use infant-specific first aid.

Full reference:
1. If coughing or crying effectively, watch carefully. Otherwise support the head and neck, place the baby face down along your forearm or thigh, head lower than chest.
2. Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.
3. If still blocked, turn face up while supporting head and neck; keep head lower than chest. Give up to 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone; follow dispatcher instructions.
4. Repeat until clear or unresponsive. If unresponsive, start infant CPR and follow dispatcher guidance.

Important:
Never use abdominal thrusts on an infant or blindly sweep the mouth.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / If coughing or crying effectively, watch carefully. Otherwise support the head and neck, place the baby face down along your forearm or thigh, head lower than chest. / Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades. / If still blocked, turn face up while supporting head and neck; keep head lower than chest. Give up to 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone; follow dispatcher instructions. / Repeat until clear or unresponsive. If unresponsive, start infant CPR and follow dispatcher guidance.

items.title: Severe allergic reaction
items.content:
When to get help:
Suspected anaphylaxis: prompt epinephrine and 911.

Full reference:
1. Look for sudden difficulty breathing, throat or tongue swelling, faintness or other signs of severe allergy.
2. Help the person use their prescribed epinephrine immediately, or administer it if trained and permitted; follow product instructions. Have someone call 911.
3. Monitor closely and follow the dispatcher for positioning and further care.
4. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

Important:
Do not wait for a rash or substitute an antihistamine for epinephrine. Seek emergency care even if symptoms improve.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Look for sudden difficulty breathing, throat or tongue swelling, faintness or other signs of severe allergy. / Help the person use their prescribed epinephrine immediately, or administer it if trained and permitted; follow product instructions. Have someone call 911.

Action 2 / Monitor closely and follow the dispatcher for positioning and further care. / If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

items.title: Possible stroke
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 immediately, even if symptoms resolve.

Full reference:
1. FACE: Ask the person to smile. Look for one-sided drooping.
2. ARMS: Ask them to lift both arms. Look for one arm drifting downward.
3. SPEECH: Ask them to repeat a simple sentence. Listen for slurring or unusual speech.
4. TIME: Note when symptoms started or when they were last known well. Share this with EMS and monitor breathing.

Important:
Do not delay calling to complete a self-test. Do not give food, drink or medication unless directed by emergency professionals.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / FACE: Ask the person to smile. Look for one-sided drooping. / ARMS: Ask them to lift both arms. Look for one arm drifting downward. / SPEECH: Ask them to repeat a simple sentence. Listen for slurring or unusual speech. / TIME: Note when symptoms started or when they were last known well. Share this with EMS and monitor breathing.

items.title: Possible poisoning
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 if collapsed, seizing, unable to wake or having trouble breathing. Otherwise contact Poison Control now.

Full reference:
1. Avoid exposing yourself. Move to fresh air for fumes if safe.
2. Call U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for individualized guidance.
3. Have the product, amount and time available if possible. Follow the specialist’s directions.
4. For eye or skin exposure, promptly rinse with running room-temperature water while arranging expert help.

Important:
Do not induce vomiting, give home remedies or attempt chemical neutralization.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Avoid exposing yourself. Move to fresh air for fumes if safe.

Action 2 / Call U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for individualized guidance.

Action 3 / Have the product, amount and time available if possible. Follow the specialist’s directions.

Action 4 / For eye or skin exposure, promptly rinse with running room-temperature water while arranging expert help.

items.title: Not breathing — infant
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 using speakerphone if possible. Begin infant CPR; have someone get an AED.

Full reference:
1. Place the infant face up on a firm, level surface.
2. Use the heel of one hand or two thumbs with hands encircling the chest, pressing on the lower half of the breastbone.
3. Give 30 compressions at 100–120 per minute, about 1½ inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Allow complete recoil.
4. If trained, keep the head neutral, lift the chin, cover the infant’s mouth and nose with your mouth and give two gentle one-second breaths, just enough for chest rise. Repeat 30:2. If unable to give breaths, continue compressions.
5. Apply an AED as soon as available; follow its prompts and use pediatric mode/pads if available. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or it is unsafe to continue.

Important:
Do not use adult compression depth. If alone without a phone after unwitnessed collapse, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call and obtain an AED. Not for resuscitation immediately after birth.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / Place the infant face up on a firm, level surface. / Use the heel of one hand or two thumbs with hands encircling the chest, pressing on the lower half of the breastbone. / Give 30 compressions at 100–120 per minute, about 1½ inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Allow complete recoil. / If trained, keep the head neutral, lift the chin, cover the infant’s mouth and nose with your mouth and give two gentle one-second breaths, just enough for chest rise. Repeat 30:2. If unable to give breaths, continue compressions. / Apply an AED as soon as available; follow its prompts and use pediatric mode/pads if available. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or it is unsafe to continue.

items.title: Use an AED
items.content:
When to get help:
For a person who will not wake up and is not breathing normally: call 911 and continue CPR while someone prepares the AED.

Full reference:
1. Switch the device on and listen to its instructions. Expose the chest and wipe it dry.
2. Apply pads to bare skin as shown on the device. For a small child or infant, prefer pediatric settings or pads when available; if pads could touch, use front-and-back placement as directed.
3. Connect pads if required. Keep everyone clear while the device checks the heart rhythm.
4. If the device advises a shock, ensure no one is touching the person; follow the shock instructions.
5. Restart CPR immediately after a shock or a no-shock prompt. Follow the AED until professional help takes over.

Important:
Do not delay CPR to search for equipment. If pediatric pads are unavailable, use adult pads that do not touch. Do not touch the person during analysis or shock.

Guided screen grouping:
Act now / Switch the device on and listen to its instructions. Expose the chest and wipe it dry. / Apply pads to bare skin as shown on the device. For a small child or infant, prefer pediatric settings or pads when available; if pads could touch, use front-and-back placement as directed. / Connect pads if required. Keep everyone clear while the device checks the heart rhythm. / If the device advises a shock, ensure no one is touching the person; follow the shock instructions. / Restart CPR immediately after a shock or a no-shock prompt. Follow the AED until professional help takes over.

items.title: Possible heart attack
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 immediately for suspected heart attack. Do not drive yourself.

Full reference:
1. Stop activity. Help the person rest in a comfortable position.
2. Arrange for an AED and stay with the person while emergency help is on the way.
3. Follow dispatcher advice about aspirin or the person’s own prescribed medication; do not delay the emergency call.
4. Watch for collapse or abnormal breathing. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

Important:
Symptoms can be subtle or occur without obvious chest pain. Do not try to diagnose a heart attack or wait for symptoms to pass.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Stop activity. Help the person rest in a comfortable position.

Action 2 / Arrange for an AED and stay with the person while emergency help is on the way.

Action 3 / Follow dispatcher advice about aspirin or the person’s own prescribed medication; do not delay the emergency call.

Action 4 / Watch for collapse or abnormal breathing. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

items.title: Seizure
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 if this is a first seizure, it lasts 5 minutes or longer, repeats before recovery, occurs in water, causes injury, or breathing or recovery is impaired. Also call for a baby under 6 months, pregnancy, diabetes with unconsciousness, or if unsure.

Full reference:
1. Note when the seizure starts. Stay nearby and clear dangerous objects away.
2. Protect the head with something soft. Loosen tight clothing around the neck.
3. If safe, gently turn the person onto their side; do not force movement.
4. After shaking stops, check breathing and responsiveness. If not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED. If breathing but not fully awake, keep on their side if safe.
5. Stay until they recover or help arrives. Follow any established emergency care plan and dispatcher instructions.

Important:
Never restrain the person, put anything in their mouth or offer food or drink before they are fully alert. If uncertain, call 911.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Note when the seizure starts. Stay nearby and clear dangerous objects away. / Protect the head with something soft. Loosen tight clothing around the neck. / If safe, gently turn the person onto their side; do not force movement.

Action 2 / After shaking stops, check breathing and responsiveness. If not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED. If breathing but not fully awake, keep on their side if safe. / Stay until they recover or help arrives. Follow any established emergency care plan and dispatcher instructions.

items.title: Asthma attack
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for severe breathing trouble, inability to speak normally, or symptoms not improving with the prescribed rescue medicine.

Full reference:
1. Help the person sit in a position that makes breathing easier; keep them calm.
2. Assist with their own quick-relief inhaler or other prescribed rescue medicine according to their care plan or dispatcher guidance. Use their spacer if available.
3. Stay with them and watch for worsening breathing, exhaustion or reduced responsiveness.
4. If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

Important:
Do not assume all breathing trouble is asthma. Do not delay emergency help while looking for medicine or waiting for improvement.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Help the person sit in a position that makes breathing easier; keep them calm.

Action 2 / Assist with their own quick-relief inhaler or other prescribed rescue medicine according to their care plan or dispatcher guidance. Use their spacer if available.

Action 3 / Stay with them and watch for worsening breathing, exhaustion or reduced responsiveness.

Action 4 / If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

items.title: Diabetic emergency
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for severe confusion, seizure, unconsciousness, abnormal breathing or inability to swallow safely.

Full reference:
1. If possible, ask about diabetes and help check blood glucose without delaying emergency care.
2. For known or suspected low blood sugar in someone fully awake and able to swallow, help them take fast-acting glucose according to their diabetes plan.
3. A common adult approach is 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, then recheck after 15 minutes and repeat if still low. Children may need a different amount; follow their plan.
4. For severe suspected low blood sugar, assist with prescribed glucagon only if trained and permitted; obtain emergency help.
5. If unconscious but breathing normally, use a safe side position. If not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

Important:
Never give anything by mouth if swallowing is unsafe. Do not give insulin based on symptoms alone. Very high blood sugar with vomiting or deep rapid breathing also needs emergency assessment.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / If possible, ask about diabetes and help check blood glucose without delaying emergency care.

Action 2 / For known or suspected low blood sugar in someone fully awake and able to swallow, help them take fast-acting glucose according to their diabetes plan.

Action 3 / A common adult approach is 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, then recheck after 15 minutes and repeat if still low. Children may need a different amount; follow their plan.

Action 4 / For severe suspected low blood sugar, assist with prescribed glucagon only if trained and permitted; obtain emergency help.

Action 5 / If unconscious but breathing normally, use a safe side position. If not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED.

items.title: Drowning emergency
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911. Do not enter dangerous water; reach or throw flotation from safety.

Full reference:
1. Get the person out of the water only if it is safe. Ask for an AED and emergency help.
2. Check responsiveness and normal breathing. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR with rescue breaths if trained.
3. A trained rescuer may start with two breaths and then give 30 compressions and two breaths repeatedly; follow age-specific CPR and dispatcher guidance. If unable to provide breaths, begin compressions immediately.
4. Use an AED as soon as possible after CPR begins; dry the chest before applying pads.
5. If breathing normally, monitor closely, keep warm and seek emergency medical assessment after a drowning event.

Important:
Do not attempt to drain water from the lungs with abdominal thrusts; do not delay CPR to obtain equipment.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Get the person out of the water only if it is safe. Ask for an AED and emergency help.

Action 2 / Check responsiveness and normal breathing. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR with rescue breaths if trained.

Action 3 / A trained rescuer may start with two breaths and then give 30 compressions and two breaths repeatedly; follow age-specific CPR and dispatcher guidance. If unable to provide breaths, begin compressions immediately.

Action 4 / Use an AED as soon as possible after CPR begins; dry the chest before applying pads.

Action 5 / If breathing normally, monitor closely, keep warm and seek emergency medical assessment after a drowning event.

items.title: Medical shock
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for suspected medical shock; treat the underlying emergency if safe.

Full reference:
1. Control severe external bleeding or give other appropriate emergency care within your training.
2. Help the person lie on their back if tolerated and there is no reason to avoid moving them. Let breathing comfort and injury precautions guide positioning.
3. Keep them comfortably warm and reassure them. If vomiting or not fully alert but breathing, protect the airway with a side position when safe.
4. Watch breathing and responsiveness until help arrives. Begin CPR and use an AED if unresponsive and not breathing normally.

Important:
Do not give food or drink. Avoid unnecessary movement if a spine injury is suspected; follow dispatcher instructions. Medical shock is not the same as emotional upset.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Control severe external bleeding or give other appropriate emergency care within your training.

Action 2 / Help the person lie on their back if tolerated and there is no reason to avoid moving them. Let breathing comfort and injury precautions guide positioning.

Action 3 / Keep them comfortably warm and reassure them. If vomiting or not fully alert but breathing, protect the airway with a side position when safe.

Action 4 / Watch breathing and responsiveness until help arrives. Begin CPR and use an AED if unresponsive and not breathing normally.

items.title: Heat burns & scalds
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for deep, extensive or circumferential burns, breathing difficulty, smoke inhalation or other severe injury. Seek urgent evaluation for burns on the face, hands, feet, joints or genitals, and burns in young children.

Full reference:
1. Stop contact with the heat source without endangering yourself.
2. Cool the affected skin promptly under clean, cool running water for 5–20 minutes. Keep the rest of the person warm, especially children.
3. Remove loose jewelry and clothing near the injury before swelling increases; leave anything stuck to skin in place.
4. After cooling, loosely protect the area with a clean, nonstick dressing. Seek medical care for blistering or concerning burns; monitor breathing.

Important:
Do not apply ice directly, butter or household remedies. Do not break blisters or peel away stuck material.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Stop contact with the heat source without endangering yourself.

Action 2 / Cool the affected skin promptly under clean, cool running water for 5–20 minutes. Keep the rest of the person warm, especially children.

Action 3 / Remove loose jewelry and clothing near the injury before swelling increases; leave anything stuck to skin in place.

Action 4 / After cooling, loosely protect the area with a clean, nonstick dressing. Seek medical care for blistering or concerning burns; monitor breathing.

items.title: Chemical burns
items.content:
When to get help:
Protect yourself. Call 911 for a chemical burn, serious exposure or breathing trouble. Begin safe decontamination immediately; Poison Control can provide substance-specific advice.

Full reference:
1. Avoid contact with the chemical; use appropriate protective equipment. Do not enter a contaminated area.
2. If safe, remove contaminated clothing and jewelry. Carefully brush loose dry chemical off skin before rinsing; avoid spreading it.
3. Rinse exposed skin with plenty of clean, room-temperature running water for at least 15 minutes, unless trained responders give different substance-specific directions.
4. For chemical exposure to an eye, use the eye injury guide and start flushing immediately. Have someone call 911 and Poison Control while rinsing.

Important:
Do not try to neutralize acids or alkalis with another chemical. Do not put creams on the area. Follow emergency responders’ instructions.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Avoid contact with the chemical; use appropriate protective equipment. Do not enter a contaminated area.

Action 2 / If safe, remove contaminated clothing and jewelry. Carefully brush loose dry chemical off skin before rinsing; avoid spreading it.

Action 3 / Rinse exposed skin with plenty of clean, room-temperature running water for at least 15 minutes, unless trained responders give different substance-specific directions.

Action 4 / For chemical exposure to an eye, use the eye injury guide and start flushing immediately. Have someone call 911 and Poison Control while rinsing.

items.title: Electrical injury
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for electrical burns, high-voltage injury, lightning injury, loss of consciousness or other serious symptoms. Do not approach a live electrical source.

Full reference:
1. Disconnect the power only if it is safe. Stay away from fallen power lines; wait for professional clearance.
2. Once the scene is safe, check responsiveness and breathing. Begin CPR and use an AED if the person is not breathing normally and is unresponsive.
3. For visible burns, use cool clean running water if safe, without delaying lifesaving care.
4. Monitor for breathing changes and shock. Obtain professional medical advice after an electrical injury, even if the skin looks normal.

Important:
Electrical injuries may damage deeper tissue or affect the heart without a large visible burn. Do not touch someone still in contact with electricity.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Disconnect the power only if it is safe. Stay away from fallen power lines; wait for professional clearance.

Action 2 / Once the scene is safe, check responsiveness and breathing. Begin CPR and use an AED if the person is not breathing normally and is unresponsive.

Action 3 / For visible burns, use cool clean running water if safe, without delaying lifesaving care.

Action 4 / Monitor for breathing changes and shock. Obtain professional medical advice after an electrical injury, even if the skin looks normal.

items.title: Possible fracture or dislocation
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for major trauma, visible deformity, bone through skin, serious bleeding, numb or cold limb, severe pain with inability to move, or unsafe transport.

Full reference:
1. Keep the injured area still in the position found. Support it gently if this does not require moving it.
2. For a closed injury, use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for up to 20 minutes.
3. If bleeding, control it with clean dressings and pressure around exposed bone; do not push bone back inside.
4. Arrange prompt medical evaluation even if the person can move the limb. Watch for changes in circulation, sensation or breathing.

Important:
Do not straighten a limb, reset a joint or test movement. A person can sometimes walk on a fracture.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Keep the injured area still in the position found. Support it gently if this does not require moving it.

Action 2 / For a closed injury, use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for up to 20 minutes.

Action 3 / If bleeding, control it with clean dressings and pressure around exposed bone; do not push bone back inside.

Action 4 / Arrange prompt medical evaluation even if the person can move the limb. Watch for changes in circulation, sensation or breathing.

items.title: Sprains, strains & bruises
items.content:
When to get help:
Seek medical evaluation for persistent or significant symptoms; call 911 for major trauma, deformity, numbness, a cold limb or unsafe transport.

Full reference:
1. Stop the activity and rest the area in a comfortable position. Treat uncertain injuries as possible fractures.
2. Place a cloth-wrapped cold pack on closed skin for no more than 20 minutes; wait at least 20 minutes before repeating.
3. Avoid painful movement and weight-bearing. Check for changes in color, feeling and temperature beyond the injury.
4. Get medical advice if pain, swelling or difficulty using the area persists or worsens.

Important:
Do not apply ice directly to bare skin. Do not force stretching or return to sports while an injury is unresolved.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Stop the activity and rest the area in a comfortable position. Treat uncertain injuries as possible fractures.

Action 2 / Place a cloth-wrapped cold pack on closed skin for no more than 20 minutes; wait at least 20 minutes before repeating.

Action 3 / Avoid painful movement and weight-bearing. Check for changes in color, feeling and temperature beyond the injury.

Action 4 / Get medical advice if pain, swelling or difficulty using the area persists or worsens.
