items.title: Cuts & scrapes
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for severe or uncontrolled bleeding or serious injury. Deep, gaping, dirty or facial wounds need prompt professional assessment.

Full reference:
1. Wash hands and use gloves if available. Stop bleeding with steady direct pressure using clean material.
2. For a minor wound once bleeding is controlled, rinse with clean running water and gently wash with mild soap.
3. Cover with a clean dressing that will not stick. Replace it if wet or dirty.
4. Seek medical advice for signs of infection, deep wounds, bites or uncertain tetanus vaccination.

Important:
Do not probe a wound or remove deeply embedded material. Severe bleeding needs immediate care, not prolonged cleaning.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Wash hands and use gloves if available. Stop bleeding with steady direct pressure using clean material.

Action 2 / For a minor wound once bleeding is controlled, rinse with clean running water and gently wash with mild soap.

Action 3 / Cover with a clean dressing that will not stick. Replace it if wet or dirty.

Action 4 / Seek medical advice for signs of infection, deep wounds, bites or uncertain tetanus vaccination.

sources.label: CDC — Tetanus prevention and wound care

items.title: Punctures & embedded objects
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for major wounds, severe bleeding, impalement or serious injury. Get prompt medical care for deep, dirty or bite punctures and retained objects.

Full reference:
1. Use gloves if available and control bleeding. For a deeply embedded object, apply pressure around it and pad around it without pushing it farther in.
2. Leave deeply lodged objects in place for trained medical personnel.
3. For a minor puncture with no retained object, rinse under clean running water for about five minutes and gently wash. Cover with a clean dressing.
4. Ask a clinician promptly about tetanus prevention, infection risk and any retained material.

Important:
Do not dig into the wound or pull out an impaled object. A small surface opening can hide a deep injury.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Use gloves if available and control bleeding. For a deeply embedded object, apply pressure around it and pad around it without pushing it farther in.

Action 2 / Leave deeply lodged objects in place for trained medical personnel.

Action 3 / For a minor puncture with no retained object, rinse under clean running water for about five minutes and gently wash. Cover with a clean dressing.

Action 4 / Ask a clinician promptly about tetanus prevention, infection risk and any retained material.

sources.label: CDC — Tetanus prevention and wound care

items.title: Possible concussion
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for worsening severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, increasing confusion, weakness, unequal pupils, slurred speech or difficulty waking. Suspected spine injury also needs emergency care.

Full reference:
1. Remove the person from activity immediately after a possible concussion. If neck or spine injury is suspected, keep them still and call 911.
2. Observe changes in alertness, balance, memory, behavior and symptoms. Arrange evaluation by a healthcare professional.
3. At school, notify the nurse or designated responder and parent/guardian according to the school emergency plan.
4. No return to sports on the day of a suspected concussion. Follow healthcare guidance for a gradual return to school and activity.

Important:
Symptoms can appear later. Do not decide that an athlete is safe to play based only on appearance or a short symptom check.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Remove the person from activity immediately after a possible concussion. If neck or spine injury is suspected, keep them still and call 911.

Action 2 / Observe changes in alertness, balance, memory, behavior and symptoms. Arrange evaluation by a healthcare professional.

Action 3 / At school, notify the nurse or designated responder and parent/guardian according to the school emergency plan.

Action 4 / No return to sports on the day of a suspected concussion. Follow healthcare guidance for a gradual return to school and activity.

sources.label: CDC HEADS UP — Sports concussion response

items.title: Head, neck & spinal injury
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 immediately if a serious head, neck or spinal injury is suspected.

Full reference:
1. Ask the person to remain still and answer verbally. Do not ask them to stand or turn their head.
2. Keep them in the position found unless moving is necessary to escape danger, perform CPR, protect the airway or control life-threatening bleeding.
3. Leave helmets and child car seats in place unless essential lifesaving care requires removal. Follow dispatcher instructions.
4. Monitor responsiveness and breathing continuously. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED.

Important:
Do not try to realign the spine or improvise a neck brace. Lifesaving care takes priority over movement precautions.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Ask the person to remain still and answer verbally. Do not ask them to stand or turn their head.

Action 2 / Keep them in the position found unless moving is necessary to escape danger, perform CPR, protect the airway or control life-threatening bleeding.

Action 3 / Leave helmets and child car seats in place unless essential lifesaving care requires removal. Follow dispatcher instructions.

Action 4 / Monitor responsiveness and breathing continuously. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED.

sources.label: Red Cross — Head, neck and spinal injury

items.title: Nosebleed
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for heavy or spurting bleeding, suspected head or spine injury, breathing difficulty, or bleeding that continues after 15 minutes of steady pressure.

Full reference:
1. If there is no suspected spine injury, sit upright with the head leaning slightly forward.
2. Pinch the soft part of the nose closed continuously for 10–15 minutes. Breathe through the mouth.
3. Avoid checking the nose repeatedly; allow the pressure time to work.
4. If bleeding stops, avoid blowing or picking the nose. Seek medical advice for repeated episodes or bleeding concerns, especially with blood thinners.

Important:
Do not tilt the head back; blood can run into the throat.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / If there is no suspected spine injury, sit upright with the head leaning slightly forward.

Action 2 / Pinch the soft part of the nose closed continuously for 10–15 minutes. Breathe through the mouth.

Action 3 / Avoid checking the nose repeatedly; allow the pressure time to work.

Action 4 / If bleeding stops, avoid blowing or picking the nose. Seek medical advice for repeated episodes or bleeding concerns, especially with blood thinners.

items.title: Eye injury or chemical splash
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for chemical eye injury, penetrating trauma, significant vision changes or severe pain. Start rinsing a chemical splash immediately while help is arranged.

Full reference:
1. For a chemical splash, begin flushing with clean room-temperature water for at least 15–20 minutes; continue as directed by responders.
2. Tilt the affected eye downward so contaminated water does not flow into the other eye. Remove contact lenses during rinsing if easy to do.
3. For an embedded object or suspected penetrating injury, do not rinse or press on the eye; obtain emergency care.
4. For persistent irritation after a minor loose particle, arrange medical care; watch for any change in vision.

Important:
Do not rub the eye or try to remove an embedded object. Do not use chemical neutralizers. Call Poison Control for exposure-specific guidance.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / For a chemical splash, begin flushing with clean room-temperature water for at least 15–20 minutes; continue as directed by responders.

Action 2 / Tilt the affected eye downward so contaminated water does not flow into the other eye. Remove contact lenses during rinsing if easy to do.

Action 3 / For an embedded object or suspected penetrating injury, do not rinse or press on the eye; obtain emergency care.

Action 4 / For persistent irritation after a minor loose particle, arrange medical care; watch for any change in vision.

sources.label: Poison Control — First aid for poisonings

items.title: Knocked-out or broken tooth
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for breathing trouble, severe bleeding or major facial/head trauma. For a knocked-out tooth, seek emergency dental care immediately.

Full reference:
1. If safe, use clean gauze to control bleeding. Find the tooth and handle only the crown, not the root.
2. For a permanent tooth, if the person is alert, cooperative and there is no aspiration risk, immediate gentle replacement may help. Do not force it; ask a dentist if uncertain.
3. If replacement is not possible, keep the tooth moist in a tooth preservation solution or milk. Bring it to the dentist promptly.
4. For a baby tooth, do not reinsert it. Contact a dentist urgently. For broken teeth, save fragments and seek dental advice.

Important:
Do not scrub the root, let the tooth dry out or store a tooth in a child’s mouth. Do not reinsert if unsure whether it is a permanent tooth.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / If safe, use clean gauze to control bleeding. Find the tooth and handle only the crown, not the root.

Action 2 / For a permanent tooth, if the person is alert, cooperative and there is no aspiration risk, immediate gentle replacement may help. Do not force it; ask a dentist if uncertain.

Action 3 / If replacement is not possible, keep the tooth moist in a tooth preservation solution or milk. Bring it to the dentist promptly.

Action 4 / For a baby tooth, do not reinsert it. Contact a dentist urgently. For broken teeth, save fragments and seek dental advice.

items.title: Heat exhaustion
items.content:
When to get help:
Get prompt medical advice. Call 911 for confusion, collapse, seizure, abnormal breathing or suspected heatstroke. Seek urgent care if vomiting, worsening or not improving with cooling.

Full reference:
1. Stop exertion and move to shade or an air-conditioned space. Stay with the person.
2. Loosen or remove excess clothing. Cool with wet skin or cloths and moving air.
3. If fully alert and able to swallow, offer frequent small sips of cool water or electrolyte drink.
4. Check for changes in alertness and breathing. If confused or collapsing, switch immediately to the heatstroke guide and call 911.

Important:
Do not send them back to sports or work that day. Do not force drinks or give salt tablets.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Stop exertion and move to shade or an air-conditioned space. Stay with the person.

Action 2 / Loosen or remove excess clothing. Cool with wet skin or cloths and moving air.

Action 3 / If fully alert and able to swallow, offer frequent small sips of cool water or electrolyte drink.

Action 4 / Check for changes in alertness and breathing. If confused or collapsing, switch immediately to the heatstroke guide and call 911.

items.title: Heatstroke
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 immediately for suspected heatstroke. Start active cooling while someone calls; do not wait for a thermometer or for sweating to stop.

Full reference:
1. Move away from heat and remove unnecessary clothing or sports equipment.
2. Cool rapidly. If safe and enough helpers are available, use supervised cool-to-cold water immersion up to the neck, keeping the airway above water. Do not immerse an unresponsive person if airway safety cannot be maintained.
3. If immersion is not safe or available, wet the skin with cool water, fan continuously and use cold wet towels or cold packs. Continue cooling until EMS takes over or directs otherwise.
4. Watch breathing and responsiveness. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED when available.

Important:
Do not give anything by mouth if mental status is altered. Do not use fever-reducing medication for heatstroke or delay cooling for transportation.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Move away from heat and remove unnecessary clothing or sports equipment.

Action 2 / Cool rapidly. If safe and enough helpers are available, use supervised cool-to-cold water immersion up to the neck, keeping the airway above water. Do not immerse an unresponsive person if airway safety cannot be maintained.

Action 3 / If immersion is not safe or available, wet the skin with cool water, fan continuously and use cold wet towels or cold packs. Continue cooling until EMS takes over or directs otherwise.

Action 4 / Watch breathing and responsiveness. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED when available.

items.title: Hypothermia
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for suspected hypothermia, especially confusion, reduced shivering, drowsiness or breathing changes. Arrange rescue rather than waiting for symptoms to worsen.

Full reference:
1. Get to shelter and shield from wind, rain and cold ground. Handle gently, particularly if very cold or confused.
2. Once protected, replace wet clothing with dry layers. Insulate the whole person, including the head, while keeping the airway clear.
3. Warm the torso gradually with blankets and wrapped warm packs. Keep insulation between packs and skin; check skin frequently.
4. Only if fully awake and swallowing normally, offer a warm nonalcoholic drink. Monitor breathing; if unresponsive and not breathing normally, follow dispatcher CPR and AED instructions.

Important:
Do not rub arms or legs, apply direct intense heat, use alcohol or put a moderately/severely hypothermic person in a hot bath. Warm the core before treating frostbite.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Get to shelter and shield from wind, rain and cold ground. Handle gently, particularly if very cold or confused.

Action 2 / Once protected, replace wet clothing with dry layers. Insulate the whole person, including the head, while keeping the airway clear.

Action 3 / Warm the torso gradually with blankets and wrapped warm packs. Keep insulation between packs and skin; check skin frequently.

Action 4 / Only if fully awake and swallowing normally, offer a warm nonalcoholic drink. Monitor breathing; if unresponsive and not breathing normally, follow dispatcher CPR and AED instructions.

sources.label: Red Cross — First aid guideline updates

items.title: Frostbite
items.content:
When to get help:
Arrange prompt medical evaluation for suspected frostbite. Call 911 for associated hypothermia, extensive injury, blistering, blackened skin or other serious symptoms.

Full reference:
1. Move to shelter. Remove wet or constricting items if they can be removed safely. Treat significant hypothermia before the frozen body part.
2. If there is no chance the area will freeze again, thaw in clean water at 99–104°F (37–40°C). If not available, allow gentle thawing in a warm room or against warm skin.
3. If refreezing is possible, protect the area without intentionally thawing it until safe shelter is reached.
4. After thawing, loosely cover with clean dry bulky dressings; separate affected digits with gauze. Protect from pressure and arrange medical care.

Important:
Never rub frozen skin, use snow or direct flame, or pop blisters. Avoid walking on frozen feet unless necessary to escape danger.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Move to shelter. Remove wet or constricting items if they can be removed safely. Treat significant hypothermia before the frozen body part.

Action 2 / If there is no chance the area will freeze again, thaw in clean water at 99–104°F (37–40°C). If not available, allow gentle thawing in a warm room or against warm skin.

Action 3 / If refreezing is possible, protect the area without intentionally thawing it until safe shelter is reached.

Action 4 / After thawing, loosely cover with clean dry bulky dressings; separate affected digits with gauze. Protect from pressure and arrange medical care.

sources.label: Red Cross — First aid guideline updates

items.title: Dehydration
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for confusion, fainting, seizure, shock or inability to stay awake. Seek prompt medical care for inability to retain fluids, very little urine, or concerning symptoms in infants or young children.

Full reference:
1. Stop activity and rest in a comfortable cool location.
2. If awake and swallowing normally, sip small amounts of fluid frequently. Use an appropriate oral rehydration solution for fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea, especially for children; follow pediatric advice.
3. Monitor urine output, alertness and worsening symptoms. Get medical advice if not improving.
4. If heat exposure is involved, check for heat exhaustion or heatstroke and use the corresponding guide.

Important:
Do not force large volumes of water, use salt tablets or give liquids to someone who cannot swallow safely. Too much water can also be dangerous.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Stop activity and rest in a comfortable cool location.

Action 2 / If awake and swallowing normally, sip small amounts of fluid frequently. Use an appropriate oral rehydration solution for fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea, especially for children; follow pediatric advice.

Action 3 / Monitor urine output, alertness and worsening symptoms. Get medical advice if not improving.

Action 4 / If heat exposure is involved, check for heat exhaustion or heatstroke and use the corresponding guide.

items.title: Suspected venomous snakebite
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 or arrange emergency evacuation immediately for a suspected venomous or unidentified snakebite, even without symptoms. Do not drive yourself.

Full reference:
1. Move away from the snake to a safe location. Keep the person still and calm while arranging emergency care.
2. Rest the bitten limb in a comfortable neutral position. Remove rings, watches or tight items before swelling increases.
3. If available, gently clean and cover with a dry clean dressing. Mark the advancing edge of swelling and note the time if this does not delay transport.
4. Report the time and circumstances. A photo from a safe distance is optional; never pursue the snake.

Important:
For U.S. snakebites, do not apply tourniquets or pressure-immobilization bandages, cut or suck the bite, apply ice or give alcohol. Do not wait for symptoms.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Move away from the snake to a safe location. Keep the person still and calm while arranging emergency care.

Action 2 / Rest the bitten limb in a comfortable neutral position. Remove rings, watches or tight items before swelling increases.

Action 3 / If available, gently clean and cover with a dry clean dressing. Mark the advancing edge of swelling and note the time if this does not delay transport.

Action 4 / Report the time and circumstances. A photo from a safe distance is optional; never pursue the snake.

items.title: Insect bites & stings
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, faintness or other signs of anaphylaxis. Seek urgent advice for numerous stings or stings inside the mouth.

Full reference:
1. Move away from insects to prevent additional stings.
2. If a bee stinger remains, remove promptly using whatever safe method is immediately available.
3. Clean the skin and apply a wrapped cold pack for short intervals for local discomfort.
4. Watch for symptoms away from the sting site. For suspected anaphylaxis, use the allergy guide, help with epinephrine as appropriate and call 911.

Important:
Do not delay epinephrine or emergency care to try an antihistamine when anaphylaxis is suspected.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Move away from insects to prevent additional stings.

Action 2 / If a bee stinger remains, remove promptly using whatever safe method is immediately available.

Action 3 / Clean the skin and apply a wrapped cold pack for short intervals for local discomfort.

Action 4 / Watch for symptoms away from the sting site. For suspected anaphylaxis, use the allergy guide, help with epinephrine as appropriate and call 911.

sources.label: Red Cross — Insect bites and stings

items.title: Tick removal & follow-up
items.content:
When to get help:
Remove an attached tick promptly. Contact a clinician about risk and preventive treatment if appropriate; seek medical care for fever, rash or illness in the following days or weeks.

Full reference:
1. With fine-point tweezers, grasp the tick as near the skin as possible.
2. Lift directly away using even pressure; avoid twisting or crushing. If small mouthparts stay in the skin and are not easily removed, leave them alone.
3. Clean hands and the site. Dispose of the tick safely or save a photo for identification. Record the date and possible exposure location.
4. Look for additional ticks and seek medical guidance if symptoms develop. Ask promptly about whether preventive antibiotics are indicated.

Important:
Do not burn the tick or apply petroleum jelly, nail polish or chemicals to make it detach. Do not wait for a rash before seeking advice about a high-risk bite.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / With fine-point tweezers, grasp the tick as near the skin as possible.

Action 2 / Lift directly away using even pressure; avoid twisting or crushing. If small mouthparts stay in the skin and are not easily removed, leave them alone.

Action 3 / Clean hands and the site. Dispose of the tick safely or save a photo for identification. Record the date and possible exposure location.

Action 4 / Look for additional ticks and seek medical guidance if symptoms develop. Ask promptly about whether preventive antibiotics are indicated.

items.title: Lightning strike
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 for any lightning strike. Ongoing lightning is a danger to rescuers; move to a safer area if necessary and safe.

Full reference:
1. Check the scene and avoid additional exposure. A lightning casualty does not retain electrical charge; touching them is safe once the scene is safe.
2. Check responsiveness and normal breathing. For someone unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR with breaths if trained, and apply an AED when available. Follow dispatcher guidance.
3. If breathing normally, assess for burns, trauma and shock; avoid unnecessary movement unless needed to escape danger or provide lifesaving care.
4. Keep the person protected from cold ground and rain, monitor breathing, and stay until responders take over.

Important:
Do not delay care because of fear that the person is electrically charged. Unlike live electrical equipment, the casualty is not a continuing electrical source.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Check the scene and avoid additional exposure. A lightning casualty does not retain electrical charge; touching them is safe once the scene is safe.

Action 2 / Check responsiveness and normal breathing. For someone unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR with breaths if trained, and apply an AED when available. Follow dispatcher guidance.

Action 3 / If breathing normally, assess for burns, trauma and shock; avoid unnecessary movement unless needed to escape danger or provide lifesaving care.

Action 4 / Keep the person protected from cold ground and rain, monitor breathing, and stay until responders take over.

sources.label: CDC — Lightning safety and first aid

items.title: Altitude illness
items.content:
When to get help:
Call 911 or activate rescue for confusion, inability to walk straight, breathlessness at rest, or severe/worsening symptoms. Arrange immediate safe descent for suspected severe altitude illness.

Full reference:
1. Stop climbing when new altitude-related symptoms appear. Rest, avoid exertion and do not ascend to sleep at a higher elevation.
2. For mild symptoms, stay at the current elevation only if stable and able to rest safely. Descend if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.
3. For confusion, poor coordination or breathing trouble at rest, descend urgently with assistance and activate rescue. Do not leave the person alone.
4. Use supplemental oxygen if available and appropriate to your training. Keep the person warm and monitor breathing until medical help is reached.

Important:
Do not push through symptoms or delay descent to try remedies. Do not force an ill person to walk if unsafe; seek assisted evacuation.

Guided screen grouping:
Action 1 / Stop climbing when new altitude-related symptoms appear. Rest, avoid exertion and do not ascend to sleep at a higher elevation.

Action 2 / For mild symptoms, stay at the current elevation only if stable and able to rest safely. Descend if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.

Action 3 / For confusion, poor coordination or breathing trouble at rest, descend urgently with assistance and activate rescue. Do not leave the person alone.

Action 4 / Use supplemental oxygen if available and appropriate to your training. Keep the person warm and monitor breathing until medical help is reached.

items.title: They won’t wake up
items.content:
Call 911 now. Ask someone to bring an AED.

Make sure the area is safe. Shout to the person and gently tap their shoulder (tap a baby’s foot). Check for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is NOT normal breathing.

Choices:
Not breathing normally → Not breathing, only gasping, or unsure whether breathing is normal → cpr-age
Breathing normally → But will not wake up → normal-breath

items.title: Start CPR now
items.content:
Call 911 on speaker if possible. Get an AED. Follow the dispatcher. Do not delay compressions.

Choose the closest age group to see the right CPR instructions.

Choices:
Teen or adult → Puberty and older → adult
Child → Age 1 to puberty → child
Baby → Under 1 year old → infant

items.title: Someone is choking
items.content:
If they cannot breathe, speak, cry or cough effectively, call 911 or have someone call now.

If they can cough strongly, encourage coughing and stay with them. For severe choking, choose an age. If the person becomes unresponsive, start CPR and follow the dispatcher.

Choices:
Age 1 or older → Child, teen or adult → choke
Baby under 1 → Infant choking first aid → baby
They are not responding → Start CPR if not breathing normally → cpr-age

items.title: Trouble breathing
items.content:
Call 911 now for severe trouble breathing or if the person cannot talk normally.

Stay with them. Help a responsive person sit in a position that makes breathing easier. Do not assume the cause.

Choices:
Severe allergic reaction → Swelling, trouble breathing or faintness → allergy
Known asthma → Wheezing or prescribed rescue inhaler → asthma
Choking → Suddenly cannot breathe or cough → choking
Not responding → Check breathing and get help → response

items.title: Other emergency
items.content:
Call 911 for immediate danger, serious injury or if you are unsure.

Pick the closest situation, or search the full library.

Choices:
Chest pain or pressure → Possible heart attack → heartattack
Sudden trouble speaking or weakness → Possible stroke → stroke
Swallowed or breathed something harmful → Poison or chemical exposure → poison
Burn → Heat or hot liquid → thermal
Head injury → Hit the head or fell → concuss
Possible broken bone → Pain, swelling or deformity → fracture
Very hot and confused → Possible heatstroke → heatstroke
Diabetic emergency → Possible serious blood sugar problem → diabetes

items.title: Get help now
items.content:
Call 911 if someone may be seriously hurt or sick, or you are not sure. Get a nearby adult.

Stay somewhere safe. Tell the dispatcher your location and what you see. Do not put yourself in danger. Follow their instructions.

Choices:
They won’t wake up → Check breathing → response
They are bleeding heavily → Apply pressure → bleed
They cannot breathe → Choking → choking
Something else → More emergency choices → more

items.title: Unresponsive but breathing normally
items.content:
Call 911 now. Keep watching their breathing.

Keep their airway clear / If safe and no suspected spine injury, place them on their side. Stay with them. Do not give food or drink.
Keep checking / If breathing stops or becomes abnormal (only gasping), start CPR and use an AED. Follow the dispatcher.

Do not move someone with a suspected spinal injury unless needed for safety, breathing or lifesaving care.

items.title: Before approaching an injured person, what should you check?
items.content:
CORRECT: Scene safety
Distractor: Whether you have a bandage
Distractor: Their age

Feedback: An unsafe scene could create another casualty.

items.title: Someone is unresponsive and only gasping. What is the priority?
items.content:
Distractor: Wait
CORRECT: Call 911, start CPR and get an AED
Distractor: Give water

Feedback: Gasping is not normal breathing.

items.title: What helps control severe external bleeding?
items.content:
Distractor: Lift the dressing repeatedly
Distractor: Rinse first
CORRECT: Firm continuous pressure and emergency help

Feedback: Maintain direct pressure while help is arranged.

items.title: Sudden facial droop and speech difficulty: what should you do?
items.content:
CORRECT: Call 911 immediately
Distractor: Wait an hour
Distractor: Let them sleep

Feedback: Stroke is time-sensitive even if symptoms improve.

items.title: Which technique must never be used on a choking infant?
items.content:
Distractor: Back blows
CORRECT: Abdominal thrusts
Distractor: Chest thrusts

Feedback: Only infant-specific techniques are appropriate.

items.title: Someone may have swallowed a harmful chemical but is awake and breathing normally. What should you do?
items.content:
Distractor: Induce vomiting
Distractor: Use a home remedy
CORRECT: Call Poison Control now

Feedback: Poison Control provides substance-specific guidance.

items.title: Someone has new chest pressure and sweating. What comes first?
items.content:
Distractor: Wait for it to pass
CORRECT: Call 911
Distractor: Have them exercise

Feedback: Suspected heart attack needs emergency assessment.

items.title: A person is having a seizure. What is a safe action?
items.content:
CORRECT: Move nearby hazards away
Distractor: Hold them down
Distractor: Place an object in their mouth

Feedback: Prevent injury without restraint or placing objects in the mouth.

items.title: Severe breathing trouble continues after a prescribed asthma rescue inhaler. What now?
items.content:
Distractor: Wait alone
Distractor: Give someone else’s medicine
CORRECT: Call 911

Feedback: Persistent or severe breathing difficulty requires urgent help.

items.title: A person with diabetes is unconscious. What should you avoid?
items.content:
Distractor: Calling 911
CORRECT: Giving food or drink by mouth
Distractor: Checking breathing

Feedback: Swallowing may be unsafe; obtain emergency assistance.

items.title: Someone is struggling in fast-moving water. What is safest for an untrained bystander?
items.content:
CORRECT: Call for help and throw flotation from safety
Distractor: Jump in
Distractor: Swim out without equipment

Feedback: Avoid becoming a second casualty.

items.title: An unresponsive person is not breathing normally after drowning. What is important?
items.content:
Distractor: Wait for the AED before CPR
Distractor: Try to drain water
CORRECT: Start CPR promptly, including breaths if trained

Feedback: Breaths and compressions are particularly important following drowning.

items.title: A person shows signs of medical shock. What should you do?
items.content:
Distractor: Give a large meal
CORRECT: Call 911, control severe bleeding and monitor
Distractor: Make them walk

Feedback: Shock can be life threatening and needs prompt care.

items.title: The AED is analyzing the heart rhythm. What should everyone do?
items.content:
CORRECT: Keep clear of the person
Distractor: Hold the person’s hands
Distractor: Remove the pads

Feedback: Avoid contact during rhythm analysis and shock.

items.title: Which depth is appropriate for infant CPR?
items.content:
Distractor: Adult depth
Distractor: No chest movement
CORRECT: About one third of chest depth, roughly 1½ inches

Feedback: Infant compressions differ from adult compressions.

items.title: A child is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Which approach is preferred if trained?
items.content:
CORRECT: CPR with compressions and breaths
Distractor: Wait for breathing to return
Distractor: Give a drink

Feedback: Breaths are especially important in pediatric CPR.

items.title: What is the preferred immediate cooling method for a heat burn?
items.content:
Distractor: Butter
CORRECT: Clean cool running water
Distractor: Direct ice

Feedback: Running water cools damaged skin without further freezing injury.

items.title: What should you avoid when a cleaner causes a chemical burn?
items.content:
CORRECT: Trying to neutralize it with another chemical
Distractor: Getting emergency help
Distractor: Using protective equipment

Feedback: Mixing chemicals can worsen the injury or create new hazards.

sources.label: Poison Control — First aid for poisonings

items.title: A person is touching a live wire. What comes first?
items.content:
Distractor: Grab their arm
CORRECT: Ensure the power is safely disconnected
Distractor: Pour water on the wire

Feedback: Approaching an energized source may injure the rescuer.

items.title: Can a person still have a fracture if they can move the limb?
items.content:
CORRECT: Yes
Distractor: No
Distractor: Only if there is bleeding

Feedback: Movement does not rule out a broken bone.

items.title: How should a cold pack be applied to a closed injury?
items.content:
Distractor: Directly against skin for an hour
CORRECT: Wrapped in cloth for up to 20 minutes
Distractor: While forcing the joint to move

Feedback: Brief, protected cooling can reduce discomfort without cold injury.

sources.label: Red Cross — Muscle, bone and joint injuries

items.title: What should you prioritize for a severely bleeding cut?
items.content:
CORRECT: Immediate bleeding control and emergency help
Distractor: Scrubbing the wound
Distractor: Looking for adhesive decorations

Feedback: Bleeding control takes precedence over cleaning.

items.title: What should you do with a deeply embedded object?
items.content:
Distractor: Pull it out
CORRECT: Leave it in place and obtain medical care
Distractor: Push it farther in

Feedback: Removal can worsen bleeding and tissue damage.

items.title: An athlete may have a concussion. Can they return to play that day if they feel better?
items.content:
Distractor: Yes
Distractor: Only if they win the game
CORRECT: No; remove them and obtain evaluation

Feedback: CDC recommends no same-day return after suspected concussion.

items.title: What should a person with a suspected spinal injury do?
items.content:
Distractor: Walk to test their legs
CORRECT: Remain still unless lifesaving care or safety requires movement
Distractor: Turn their head to find the pain

Feedback: Unnecessary movement can worsen a spinal injury.

sources.label: Red Cross — Head, neck and spinal injury

items.title: Which position is appropriate for an uncomplicated nosebleed?
items.content:
Distractor: Head tilted back
Distractor: Lying flat
CORRECT: Sitting and leaning slightly forward

Feedback: Leaning forward helps keep blood out of the throat.

items.title: What is the immediate response to a chemical splash in an eye?
items.content:
Distractor: Rub it
CORRECT: Flush with clean water while help is arranged
Distractor: Wait until pain stops

Feedback: Prompt irrigation reduces chemical contact time.

items.title: Should a knocked-out baby tooth be pushed back into its socket?
items.content:
Distractor: Yes
CORRECT: No; contact a dentist
Distractor: Only after scrubbing it

Feedback: Reinserting a baby tooth can injure the developing permanent tooth.

items.title: An athlete is sweaty and dizzy but alert. What should happen first?
items.content:
Distractor: Continue practice
CORRECT: Stop activity and move somewhere cool
Distractor: Take salt tablets

Feedback: Rest and cooling are initial priorities; monitor for signs of heatstroke.

items.title: A runner in hot weather becomes confused. What is the priority?
items.content:
CORRECT: Call 911 and begin rapid cooling
Distractor: Wait until their skin becomes dry
Distractor: Give fever medicine

Feedback: Altered awareness during heat exposure is a medical emergency; cooling and emergency activation are immediate priorities.

items.title: Where should you focus gentle rewarming for hypothermia?
items.content:
Distractor: Hands and feet first
Distractor: A hot bath immediately
CORRECT: Torso, with protection from further heat loss

Feedback: Insulation and controlled core warming reduce further cooling and avoid harmful aggressive peripheral warming.

items.title: When is intentional frostbite thawing appropriate?
items.content:
CORRECT: When refreezing can be prevented
Distractor: While still exposed to freezing weather
Distractor: After rubbing with snow

Feedback: Thawing followed by refreezing can greatly worsen tissue injury.

items.title: A fully alert person with mild fluid loss can swallow. Which response is appropriate?
items.content:
Distractor: Force a gallon of water at once
CORRECT: Offer small frequent sips
Distractor: Avoid all fluids

Feedback: Small, frequent amounts help replace losses without forcing excessive water.

items.title: What should you do after a suspected rattlesnake bite?
items.content:
Distractor: Wait to see if swelling starts
Distractor: Use a suction kit
CORRECT: Arrange emergency care immediately and limit movement

Feedback: Early medical treatment is essential even when initial symptoms are mild.

items.title: A bee sting is followed by throat swelling. Which guide is most important?
items.content:
CORRECT: Anaphylaxis / severe allergic reaction
Distractor: Frostbite
Distractor: Sprain

Feedback: Throat swelling after a sting may indicate anaphylaxis and requires immediate emergency response.

sources.label: Red Cross — Insect bites and stings

items.title: What is the preferred way to remove an attached tick?
items.content:
Distractor: Cover it in petroleum jelly
CORRECT: Use fine-tipped tweezers near the skin and pull steadily
Distractor: Burn it with a match

Feedback: Prompt removal with tweezers avoids unnecessary delay and injury.

items.title: Once the scene is safe, is it safe to touch a lightning-strike casualty?
items.content:
Distractor: No, they retain electricity
Distractor: Only with rubber gloves
CORRECT: Yes, they do not retain an electrical charge

Feedback: Lightning casualties do not store a charge; ongoing storms are the scene hazard.

sources.label: CDC — Lightning safety and first aid

items.title: A hiker develops confusion and cannot walk straight at high altitude. What should the group do?
items.content:
Distractor: Climb higher to acclimatize
CORRECT: Activate rescue and arrange immediate safe descent
Distractor: Wait until morning with no monitoring

Feedback: Neurological symptoms at altitude can signal a life-threatening emergency requiring descent and evacuation.

items.title: Collapse in the hallway — decision 1
items.content:
An adult collapses in a clear hallway. They do not respond and are only gasping.

Which emergency choice fits?
CORRECT: Not responding / not breathing normally
Distractor: Seizure
Distractor: Minor injury

Feedback: Gasping is not normal breathing. Get help immediately.

items.title: Collapse in the hallway — decision 2
items.content:
An adult collapses in a clear hallway. They do not respond and are only gasping.

What should happen now?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911, send for an AED and begin CPR following dispatcher guidance.
Distractor: Wait for the nurse before doing anything.
Distractor: Give the person water.

Feedback: Calling for help and starting CPR must not be delayed. Follow the dispatcher and AED.

items.title: Lunchroom emergency — decision 1
items.content:
A classmate suddenly cannot speak, cough effectively or breathe while eating.

Which emergency choice fits?
CORRECT: Choking
Distractor: Other injury
Distractor: Seizure

Feedback: Inability to speak or breathe can indicate severe choking.

sources.label: Red Cross — Adult and child choking

items.title: Lunchroom emergency — decision 2
items.content:
A classmate suddenly cannot speak, cough effectively or breathe while eating.

Which response should you practice?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911 and get help. Give age-appropriate back blows and thrusts as instructed.
Distractor: Give water to wash the food down.
Distractor: Reach into the mouth without seeing an object.

Feedback: Get emergency help promptly; use appropriate choking first aid, never a blind finger sweep.

sources.label: Red Cross — Adult and child choking

items.title: Accident in the workshop — decision 1
items.content:
A student has a deep arm wound with heavy, continuous bleeding. The machine is switched off and the area is safe.

Which emergency choice fits?
CORRECT: Severe bleeding
Distractor: Trouble breathing
Distractor: Minor scrape

Feedback: Heavy ongoing bleeding can be life-threatening.

items.title: Accident in the workshop — decision 2
items.content:
A student has a deep arm wound with heavy, continuous bleeding. The machine is switched off and the area is safe.

What is a priority?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911 and apply firm direct pressure with a dressing if safe.
Distractor: Rinse the wound instead of controlling the bleeding.
Distractor: Keep lifting the dressing to check every few seconds.

Feedback: Control life-threatening bleeding promptly and use dispatcher guidance.

items.title: Seizure during class — decision 1
items.content:
A student falls and begins jerking. An adult says this is their first known seizure.

What should you do first?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911, clear nearby hazards and get an adult.
Distractor: Hold the student down.
Distractor: Put an object between their teeth.

Feedback: A first known seizure needs emergency help. Protect them from nearby hazards without restraint.

items.title: Seizure during class — decision 2
items.content:
A student falls and begins jerking. An adult says this is their first known seizure.

What information helps responders?
CORRECT: When the seizure started and whether breathing returns to normal.
Distractor: The student’s grades.
Distractor: How many classmates watched.

Feedback: Time the seizure if possible and observe breathing; do not delay getting help.

items.title: Allergic reaction at lunch — decision 1
items.content:
A student develops swollen lips, difficulty breathing and widespread hives after eating. They have their prescribed auto-injector.

Which emergency category fits?
CORRECT: Trouble breathing / severe allergic reaction
Distractor: Minor skin irritation
Distractor: Fracture

Feedback: Breathing trouble with allergy symptoms may be anaphylaxis.

items.title: Allergic reaction at lunch — decision 2
items.content:
A student develops swollen lips, difficulty breathing and widespread hives after eating. They have their prescribed auto-injector.

What should happen now?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911 and get help with their prescribed epinephrine following the device and dispatcher instructions.
Distractor: Wait to see if the symptoms pass.
Distractor: Offer another bite of food.

Feedback: Anaphylaxis can progress rapidly; emergency help and prompt prescribed epinephrine are important.

items.title: AED has arrived — decision 1
items.content:
An adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Someone has called emergency services and another person brings an AED.

What should the helper do?
CORRECT: Turn on the AED and follow its prompts.
Distractor: Put the AED beside the person and wait.
Distractor: Wait until the person wakes up.

Feedback: The AED guides the user through its operation. Minimize interruptions to CPR.

items.title: AED has arrived — decision 2
items.content:
An adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Someone has called emergency services and another person brings an AED.

The AED says it is analyzing. What now?
CORRECT: Make sure nobody touches the person while it analyzes and follow its instructions.
Distractor: Keep a hand on the person to steady them.
Distractor: Turn the AED off.

Feedback: Stay clear when the device analyzes or delivers a shock, then follow its prompts to resume CPR.

items.title: Infant choking — decision 1
items.content:
A baby is awake but cannot cry, cough effectively or breathe.

Which age-specific pathway fits?
CORRECT: Infant choking (under 1 year)
Distractor: Adult choking
Distractor: Adult CPR

Feedback: Infants require a different choking response than older children or adults.

items.title: Infant choking — decision 2
items.content:
A baby is awake but cannot cry, cough effectively or breathe.

Which technique sequence is appropriate?
CORRECT: Get emergency help and alternate 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts as instructed.
Distractor: Use abdominal thrusts on the baby.
Distractor: Try to sweep the mouth even if no object is visible.

Feedback: Use infant-specific care, not abdominal thrusts or blind finger sweeps. If the infant becomes unresponsive, start CPR as directed.

items.title: Hot pan burn — decision 1
items.content:
A small area of an adult’s forearm touches a hot pan. They are awake and breathing normally.

What is the best immediate cooling choice?
CORRECT: Cool, clean running water.
Distractor: Ice directly on the burn.
Distractor: Butter or cooking oil.

Feedback: Cool water helps limit thermal injury. Ice and greasy substances are not appropriate initial care.

items.title: Hot pan burn — decision 2
items.content:
A small area of an adult’s forearm touches a hot pan. They are awake and breathing normally.

What should you do if a burn is large, deep or involves the face?
CORRECT: Get urgent emergency help as appropriate.
Distractor: Ignore it because the pain might fade.
Distractor: Pop any blisters.

Feedback: Serious burns require professional evaluation; do not intentionally break blisters.

items.title: Unknown medicine — decision 1
items.content:
A younger child may have swallowed an unknown amount of medicine. They are awake and breathing normally.

Who should an adult contact promptly for expert guidance?
CORRECT: Poison Control (simulated).
Distractor: A friend who has taken the medicine.
Distractor: Nobody unless symptoms appear.

Feedback: Poison Control provides case-specific guidance even before symptoms appear. Call 911 for collapse, seizure, trouble breathing or inability to awaken.

items.title: Unknown medicine — decision 2
items.content:
A younger child may have swallowed an unknown amount of medicine. They are awake and breathing normally.

What should you avoid?
CORRECT: Do not make the child vomit.
Distractor: Keep the packaging for the adult or specialist.
Distractor: Tell an adult what happened.

Feedback: Inducing vomiting can make poisoning worse. Keep information available for the specialist.

items.title: Sudden changes in speech — decision 1
items.content:
An older relative suddenly has a drooping face, weak arm and slurred speech.

What is the priority?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911 for possible stroke.
Distractor: Wait until tomorrow.
Distractor: Ask them to walk around until it improves.

Feedback: Sudden face, arm or speech changes are stroke warning signs; get emergency help.

items.title: Sudden changes in speech — decision 2
items.content:
An older relative suddenly has a drooping face, weak arm and slurred speech.

What information is especially useful?
CORRECT: When they were last known to be normal.
Distractor: What they ate last week.
Distractor: How many steps they can walk now.

Feedback: The last-known-well time can help clinicians choose treatment. Do not delay transport or give food or drink.

items.title: Hard collision during a game — decision 1
items.content:
A player is dizzy and has a headache after a collision. They are awake, breathing and have no stated emergency danger signs.

What should happen now?
CORRECT: Remove them from play and tell the coach or adult.
Distractor: Let them finish the game.
Distractor: Ask them to prove they are fine by running.

Feedback: A possible concussion requires immediate removal from play and assessment.

items.title: Hard collision during a game — decision 2
items.content:
A player is dizzy and has a headache after a collision. They are awake, breathing and have no stated emergency danger signs.

When may they return to sports?
CORRECT: After appropriate healthcare clearance and a supervised return process.
Distractor: As soon as the next match starts.
Distractor: Whenever they say they feel tough enough.

Feedback: Do not return a player with suspected concussion to play that day; follow healthcare guidance.

items.title: Confusion on a hot field — decision 1
items.content:
During outdoor practice, a player becomes very hot and confused.

Which response fits?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911 for possible heatstroke.
Distractor: Wait in the sun until practice ends.
Distractor: Tell them to run another lap.

Feedback: Confusion with heat exposure is an emergency warning sign.

items.title: Confusion on a hot field — decision 2
items.content:
During outdoor practice, a player becomes very hot and confused.

While help is coming, what is a priority?
CORRECT: Start rapid cooling safely, with adult help and dispatcher guidance.
Distractor: Wrap them in a heavy blanket.
Distractor: Force them to drink while confused.

Feedback: Rapid cooling is important. Do not force fluids on someone who is not fully alert.

items.title: Injured wrist — decision 1
items.content:
A player falls and has a very painful, visibly bent wrist.

What should you do?
CORRECT: Get adult and medical help; keep the wrist supported as found.
Distractor: Pull it straight.
Distractor: Ask them to keep playing.

Feedback: Do not straighten a suspected fracture. Severe deformity or other danger signs need urgent help.

items.title: Injured wrist — decision 2
items.content:
A player falls and has a very painful, visibly bent wrist.

Which observation is worth reporting?
CORRECT: Numbness, color change or cold fingers.
Distractor: The color of their shoes.
Distractor: The final score.

Feedback: Changes beyond the injury can suggest circulation or nerve problems.

items.title: Breathing trouble at an event — decision 1
items.content:
A participant with asthma is struggling to breathe and cannot speak in full sentences.

Which response should you choose?
CORRECT: Simulate calling 911 and get help for severe breathing difficulty.
Distractor: Tell them to lie down and wait alone.
Distractor: Ask them to keep exercising.

Feedback: Severe breathing trouble requires immediate emergency help.

items.title: Breathing trouble at an event — decision 2
items.content:
A participant with asthma is struggling to breathe and cannot speak in full sentences.

What is appropriate while help comes?
CORRECT: Help them use their own prescribed rescue medicine as directed, with adult or dispatcher help.
Distractor: Share a random medication.
Distractor: Make them run to clear their lungs.

Feedback: Assist with their prescribed rescue medicine when appropriate; follow their plan and dispatcher guidance.

items.title: Tick after a hike — decision 1
items.content:
After a hike, an adult notices an attached tick on their leg.

Which tool is appropriate?
CORRECT: Fine-tipped tweezers.
Distractor: A lit match.
Distractor: Nail polish.

Feedback: Remove an attached tick promptly with suitable tweezers.

items.title: Tick after a hike — decision 2
items.content:
After a hike, an adult notices an attached tick on their leg.

How should it be removed?
CORRECT: Grip close to the skin and pull upward steadily.
Distractor: Twist the tick repeatedly.
Distractor: Coat it with petroleum jelly and wait.

Feedback: Clean the area after removal and seek medical advice for concerning symptoms.

items.title: Cold and confused — decision 1
items.content:
A hiker is wet, very cold, confused and stumbling.

What should you do?
CORRECT: Get emergency help for possible hypothermia.
Distractor: Tell them to keep hiking alone.
Distractor: Give them an alcoholic drink.

Feedback: Confusion in the cold can indicate dangerous hypothermia.

items.title: Cold and confused — decision 2
items.content:
A hiker is wet, very cold, confused and stumbling.

What helps while arranging rescue?
CORRECT: Move to shelter if safe, handle gently and insulate with dry layers.
Distractor: Rub the skin vigorously.
Distractor: Put bare skin against a very hot surface.

Feedback: Prevent further heat loss; avoid rough handling and burns.

items.title: Danger near the road — decision 1
items.content:
You see someone injured beside a road with traffic still moving close to them.

What is the first priority?
CORRECT: Stay safe and get emergency help from a safe location.
Distractor: Run into traffic immediately.
Distractor: Stand in the traffic lane to film.

Feedback: Do not enter a dangerous scene or become another casualty.

items.title: Danger near the road — decision 2
items.content:
You see someone injured beside a road with traffic still moving close to them.

What should you tell the simulated dispatcher?
CORRECT: Location, hazards, what happened and what you can see.
Distractor: Just your favorite hiking trail.
Distractor: Hang up before answering questions.

Feedback: Give a clear location and follow dispatcher instructions.

items.title: Person struggling in water — decision 1
items.content:
Someone is struggling in deep water. You are on shore and have no rescue training.

How should you help?
CORRECT: Call for trained help; reach or throw a flotation aid from a safe position if possible.
Distractor: Jump in without equipment or training.
Distractor: Walk away without alerting anyone.

Feedback: Avoid becoming another drowning victim. Get rescue help promptly.

items.title: Person struggling in water — decision 2
items.content:
Someone is struggling in deep water. You are on shore and have no rescue training.

Once trained rescuers bring an unresponsive nonbreathing person to safety, what matters?
CORRECT: Emergency services, CPR including breaths as trained or dispatcher-guided, and an AED.
Distractor: Wait for them to cough before calling.
Distractor: Try to drain water by hanging them upside down.

Feedback: Drowning resuscitation needs rapid emergency response and ventilation as well as compressions.

items.title: Protective gloves — decision 1
items.content:
You are selecting supplies for a first-aid kit.

What helps reduce direct contact with blood?
CORRECT: Disposable protective gloves
Distractor: A flashlight
Distractor: A roll of string

Feedback: Use gloves if available, without delaying lifesaving care.

items.title: Identify an AED — decision 1
items.content:
A helper asks what equipment to bring for suspected cardiac arrest.

Which device analyzes heart rhythm and may deliver a shock?
CORRECT: Automated external defibrillator (AED)
Distractor: Digital thermometer
Distractor: Cold pack

Feedback: An AED provides prompts and can deliver a shock when indicated.

items.title: Bleeding supplies — decision 1
items.content:
You are choosing something to apply direct pressure to a wound.

Which item is suitable if available?
CORRECT: Clean gauze or dressing
Distractor: A loose bag of ice
Distractor: An electrical cable

Feedback: A clean dressing can be used for firm direct pressure.

items.title: Recognize a tourniquet — decision 1
items.content:
You are reviewing bleeding-control equipment with an instructor.

What is a commercial tourniquet intended for?
CORRECT: Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg when appropriate.
Distractor: A small paper cut.
Distractor: A neck wound.

Feedback: Tourniquets are for appropriate severe limb bleeding. Learn use with certified training and follow dispatcher instructions.

items.title: Small tools — decision 1
items.content:
You are selecting a tool for tick removal practice.

Which item is appropriate?
CORRECT: Fine-tipped tweezers
Distractor: A heating pad
Distractor: A tourniquet

Feedback: Use tweezers to grasp the tick close to the skin.

items.title: Cold pack — decision 1
items.content:
A coach wants to apply a cold pack to a closed injury while arranging appropriate care.

What should go between the pack and skin?
CORRECT: A thin dry towel.
Distractor: Nothing; apply frozen material directly.
Distractor: A layer of hot oil.

Feedback: A cloth barrier helps protect the skin.

items.title: Emergency blanket — decision 1
items.content:
You are reviewing a cold-weather kit.

What is a dry blanket useful for?
CORRECT: Reducing further heat loss.
Distractor: Treating heatstroke by trapping heat.
Distractor: Replacing a call for rescue.

Feedback: Insulation helps reduce heat loss; emergency care may still be needed.

items.title: Time a seizure — decision 1
items.content:
A teacher is practicing recording events for responders.

Which tool helps record elapsed seizure time?
CORRECT: A stopwatch or timer.
Distractor: An AED shock button.
Distractor: A thermometer.

Feedback: Timing helps communicate duration, but never delay care or calling for help to start it.

items.title: home
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
What is happening? Get a nearby adult or another helper. If someone is in danger or you are unsure, call 911 now. Choose not responding, choking, severe bleeding, seizure, trouble breathing, or other emergency. You can also choose I do not know what to do, or I have an AED.

Speech-engine script:
What is happening? Get a nearby adult or another helper. If someone is in danger or you are unsure, call nine one one now. Choose not responding, choking, severe bleeding, seizure, trouble breathing, or other emergency. You can also choose I do not know what to do, or I have an A E D.

items.content:

Call 911 now. Ask someone to bring an AED. Make sure the area is safe. Shout to the person and gently tap their shoulder (tap a baby’s foot). Check for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is NOT normal breathing. Choose: Not breathing normally Breathing normally

Speech-engine script:

items.title: cpr-age-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Call 911 on speaker if possible. Get an AED. Follow the dispatcher. Do not delay compressions. Choose the closest age group to see the right CPR instructions. Choose: Teen or adult Child Baby

Speech-engine script:
Call nine one one on speaker if possible. Get an A E D. Follow the dispatcher. Do not delay compressions. Choose the closest age group to see the right C P R instructions. Choose: Teen or adult Child Baby

items.title: choking-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
If they cannot breathe, speak, cry or cough effectively, call 911 or have someone call now. If they can cough strongly, encourage coughing and stay with them. For severe choking, choose an age. If the person becomes unresponsive, start CPR and follow the dispatcher. Choose: Age 1 or older Baby under 1 They are not responding

Speech-engine script:

For severe choking, choose an age. If the person becomes unresponsive, start C P R and follow the dispatcher. Choose: Age 1 or older Baby under 1 They are not responding

items.title: breathing-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Call 911 now for severe trouble breathing or if the person cannot talk normally. Stay with them. Help a responsive person sit in a position that makes breathing easier. Do not assume the cause. Choose: Severe allergic reaction Known asthma Choking Not responding

Speech-engine script:
Call nine one one now for severe trouble breathing or if the person cannot talk normally. Stay with them. Help a responsive person sit in a position that makes breathing easier. Do not assume the cause. Choose: Severe allergic reaction Known asthma Choking Not responding

items.title: more-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Call 911 for immediate danger, serious injury or if you are unsure. Pick the closest situation, or search the full library. Choose: Chest pain or pressure Sudden trouble speaking or weakness Swallowed or breathed something harmful Burn Head injury Possible broken bone Very hot and confused Diabetic emergency

Speech-engine script:
Call nine one one for immediate danger, serious injury or if you are unsure. Pick the closest situation, or search the full library. Choose: Chest pain or pressure Sudden trouble speaking or weakness Swallowed or breathed something harmful Burn Head injury Possible broken bone Very hot and confused Diabetic emergency

items.title: unsure-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Call 911 if someone may be seriously hurt or sick, or you are not sure. Get a nearby adult. Stay somewhere safe. Tell the dispatcher your location and what you see. Do not put yourself in danger. Follow their instructions. Choose: They won’t wake up They are bleeding heavily They cannot breathe Something else

Speech-engine script:
Call nine one one if someone may be seriously hurt or sick, or you are not sure. Get a nearby adult. Stay somewhere safe. Tell the dispatcher your location and what you see. Do not put yourself in danger. Follow their instructions. Choose: They won’t wake up They are bleeding heavily They cannot breathe Something else

items.title: first-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call 911 for a life-threatening condition. Check for hazards before approaching. Use protective equipment if available. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

Speech-engine script:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call nine one one for a life-threatening condition. Check for hazards before approaching. Use protective equipment if available. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

items.title: first-1
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call 911 for a life-threatening condition. Check responsiveness and normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds; look for severe bleeding. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

Speech-engine script:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call nine one one for a life-threatening condition. Check responsiveness and normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds; look for severe bleeding. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

items.title: first-2
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call 911 for a life-threatening condition. Call 911 or ask someone to call and bring an AED. Follow the dispatcher. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

Speech-engine script:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call nine one one for a life-threatening condition. Call nine one one or ask someone to call and bring an A E D. Follow the dispatcher. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

items.title: first-3
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call 911 for a life-threatening condition. If unresponsive and not breathing normally (including only gasping), start CPR and use an AED as soon as possible. Give other care within your training. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

Speech-engine script:
Do not enter an unsafe scene. Call nine one one for a life-threatening condition. If unresponsive and not breathing normally (including only gasping), start C P R and use an A E D as soon as possible. Give other care within your training. Important. If unresponsive but breathing normally, keep the airway clear and use a side recovery position if safe; monitor breathing. Gasping is not normal breathing. Do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury unless safety or lifesaving care requires it.

items.title: adult-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Call 911 and get an AED. Start CPR immediately. Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface. Put the heel of one hand in the center of the chest and the other hand on top. Press hard and fast at 100–120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep, avoiding more than 2.4 inches. Allow full chest recoil. If trained, give 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. If unable or unwilling to give breaths, continue chest compressions. Turn on the AED as soon as available and follow its spoken instructions. Continue until professionals take over, normal breathing returns or you cannot continue safely. Important. For children or babies open the corresponding child or infant CPR guide. Rescue breaths are especially important for drowning-related and pediatric arrests.

Speech-engine script:
Call nine one one and get an A E D. Start C P R immediately. Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface. Put the heel of one hand in the center of the chest and the other hand on top. Press hard and fast at 100 to 120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep, avoiding more than 2.4 inches. Allow full chest recoil. If trained, give 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. If unable or unwilling to give breaths, continue chest compressions. Turn on the A E D as soon as available and follow its spoken instructions. Continue until professionals take over, normal breathing returns or you cannot continue safely. Important. For children or babies open the corresponding child or infant C P R guide. Rescue breaths are especially important for drowning-related and pediatric arrests.

items.title: child-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Call 911 using speakerphone if possible. Start CPR; ask someone to bring an AED. Lay the child face up on a hard, level surface. Place one or both hands on the lower half of the breastbone, depending on the child’s size. Give 30 compressions at 100–120 per minute, about 2 inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Let the chest fully rise between presses. If trained, open the airway with a gentle head tilt and chin lift, pinch the nose and give 2 breaths, each over about one second, enough for visible chest rise. Repeat 30:2. If unable to give breaths, keep compressing. Use an AED when available; follow its prompts. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or you cannot safely continue. Important. If alone without a phone, dispatcher activation timing depends on whether collapse was witnessed; if unwitnessed, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call and obtain an AED. Use infant CPR for a baby under 1.

Speech-engine script:
Call nine one one using speakerphone if possible. Start C P R; ask someone to bring an A E D. Lay the child face up on a hard, level surface. Place one or both hands on the lower half of the breastbone, depending on the child’s size. Give 30 compressions at 100 to 120 per minute, about 2 inches deep (one-third of chest depth). Let the chest fully rise between presses. If trained, open the airway with a gentle head tilt and chin lift, pinch the nose and give 2 breaths, each over about one second, enough for visible chest rise. Repeat thirty compressions to two breaths. If unable to give breaths, keep compressing. Use an A E D when available; follow its prompts. Continue until normal breathing returns, help takes over or you cannot safely continue. Important. If alone without a phone, dispatcher activation timing depends on whether collapse was witnessed; if unwitnessed, give about 2 minutes of C P R before leaving to call and obtain an A E D. Use infant C P R for a baby under 1.

items.title: bleed-0
items.content:
Displayed transcript:
Call 911 and apply firm pressure immediately. Wear gloves or use a barrier if possible. Locate the source of bleeding. Press firmly and continuously with gauze or clean cloth. If an object is stuck in the wound, press around it, not on it. For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, apply a manufactured tourniquet if available and trained; follow dispatcher or device instructions. Keep the person warm and monitor breathing and responsiveness until help arrives. Important. Do not remove an embedded object; press around it. Do not loosen an applied tourniquet.

Speech-engine script:

items.title: Practice a responsible emergency call — decision 1
items.content:
In this fictional exercise, a classmate collapses and needs immediate help. No real call is made.

You think emergency help is needed, but you are not completely sure. What should you do?
CORRECT: Ask someone to call 911 now or call yourself; get help and follow dispatcher instructions.
Distractor: Wait until you are absolutely certain.
Distractor: Call as a joke to see what happens.

Feedback: Do not delay a good-faith call when someone may need immediate emergency assistance. Never prank call.

items.title: Practice a responsible emergency call — decision 2
items.content:
In this fictional exercise, a classmate collapses and needs immediate help. No real call is made.

What should you tell the simulated dispatcher first?
CORRECT: Your exact location and what happened; answer their questions and stay on the line.
Distractor: Only your first name, then hang up.
Distractor: Make up an address.

Feedback: Accurate location and emergency details help responders reach the person. Follow the dispatcher.

items.title: Accidental emergency call — decision 1
items.content:
Imagine you accidentally called 911 while trying to use the phone. This is a practice scenario only.

What is the right response if the call connects?
CORRECT: Stay on the line and explain the accident.
Distractor: Hang up immediately without speaking.
Distractor: Pretend there is an emergency.

Feedback: Explain an accidental call honestly. Hanging up can cause unnecessary follow-up.

items.title: Single deliberate call confirmation and fallback
items.content:
Real emergency call
You are about to contact real emergency services, not practice.
If someone may need immediate help, call now. You do not have to be certain.
No prank calls.
Intentionally false reports can delay lifesaving help and may result in school discipline, criminal charges or response costs.
Continue to 911
Cancel — return to first aid
Can't reach 911?
If you call accidentally, stay on the line and explain the mistake. Do not hang up.
Can't reach 911?
Keep trying to get help. Do not delay lifesaving first aid.
← Return to first aid
Try 911 even if your carrier has no signal. Another compatible network may connect. Tell responders your exact location.
Ask a nearby adult or bystander to call from another phone and bring an AED if needed. At school, alert the office or nurse.
If you cannot call, try texting 911 where supported. Give your location and emergency. If delivery fails, find another way to get help. Texting requires a connection.
Outdoors, use an available satellite emergency SOS device, rescue beacon or rescue plan. If safe, send someone for help. Avoid additional danger.
Continue appropriate first aid while help is sought. Follow the dispatcher or AED when available.
This app cannot send a distress signal, locate you, place a call on your behalf or guarantee a connection. For medical guidance, use established resources and training.
